subtopics.name: Using Ratio Analysis To Make Strategic Decisions

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** way in which a business could improve its rate of inventory turnover.
parts.solution_md:
The rate of inventory turnover shows how many times a business sells and replaces its inventory in a year, so it improves when the same level of sales is achieved from a smaller average inventory **[1]**. One way is to identify slow-moving lines and discount them to clear the stock **[1]**. This reduces average inventory immediately, releases cash and storage space, and stops the business reordering items that were never selling, so the ratio improves for a genuine reason rather than as a one-off effect **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The rate of inventory turnover improves when average inventory falls relative to cost of sales
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Clearing slow-moving or obsolete lines through discounting reduces average inventory
> - Ordering smaller quantities more frequently, as under just in time, cuts the inventory held
> - Improving demand forecasting reduces over-ordering
> - Better warehouse systems identify stock that is not moving
> - More effective promotion raises sales without increasing inventory
> - Reducing the product range concentrates sales on fewer lines
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Know which half of the ratio you are changing. Cost of sales sits on top and average inventory underneath, so a business improves the figure either by selling more or by holding less, and a strong answer says which of the two it is doing. Naming the half you are moving keeps the chain of reasoning straight.

parts.problem_md: Explain why a business monitors its trade payables turnover.
parts.solution_md:
Trade payables turnover measures the average number of days a business takes to pay its suppliers **[1]**. A business monitors it because taking longer to pay keeps cash inside the business for longer, which improves liquidity without any need to borrow **[1]**. However, if the figure rises too far, suppliers may withdraw credit terms, demand payment in advance or give priority to other customers, so the business watches the ratio in order to take the cash benefit without damaging the relationships it depends on **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Trade payables turnover shows the average number of days taken to pay suppliers
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Paying more slowly retains cash in the business, improving liquidity at no interest cost
> - A rising figure may signal to suppliers that the business is struggling
> - Suppliers may withdraw credit, shorten terms or require payment in advance
> - Early payment discounts may be lost by paying too slowly
> - Comparing payables days with receivables days shows whether cash leaves before it arrives
> - A very low figure may mean cash is going out faster than it needs to
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most ratios have an optimum rather than a direction. Neither a rising nor a falling payables figure is automatically good, and answers that simply argue "higher is better" tend to stop at one mark. The marks come from showing what goes wrong if the figure moves too far either way, which is exactly why the business monitors it.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'trade receivables turnover'.
parts.solution_md:
Trade receivables turnover measures the average number of days a business takes to collect the money owed to it by credit customers **[1]**, calculated by dividing trade receivables by revenue and multiplying by 365 **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The average number of days customers take to pay what they owe
> - Trade receivables divided by revenue, multiplied by 365
> - A measure of how quickly a business converts credit sales into cash
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Say whose money it is and which way it moves. Receivables are owed to the business by its customers; payables are owed by the business to its suppliers. These two ratios are easy to reverse under pressure, and a definition that swaps them describes the opposite side of the business entirely.

parts.problem_md: Explain why financial efficiency is important to a business.
parts.solution_md:
Financial efficiency measures how well a business manages the working capital tied up in its inventory, its customers and its suppliers **[1]**. It matters because a business can be profitable and still run out of cash: money sitting in unsold stock, or in invoices customers have not yet paid, cannot be used to pay wages or suppliers **[1]**. Improving these ratios releases cash the business already owns, which is cheaper than borrowing and avoids the interest costs that would otherwise reduce profit **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Financial efficiency measures how effectively a business manages inventory, trade receivables and trade payables
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Cash tied up in inventory or in unpaid invoices is not available for day-to-day payments
> - A profitable business can still fail if its working capital is managed badly
> - Releasing cash from working capital is cheaper than borrowing the same amount
> - Collecting from customers faster reduces the risk of bad debts
> - Efficient inventory management cuts storage, insurance and obsolescence costs
> - The ratios show whether a growing business can fund its growth from its own operations
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Efficiency ratios are about speed, not size. They measure how quickly money moves through the business, not how much of it there is. A business holding large inventories is not automatically inefficient; one that takes a long time to sell them is. Keeping that distinction clear stops the answer drifting into a general discussion of costs.

parts.problem_md: Define the term ‘liquidity ratio’.
parts.solution_md:
A liquidity ratio is a financial ratio that measures whether a business has enough short-term assets **[1]** to pay off its short-term debts **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A financial ratio that assesses the short-term financial strength of a business, measuring its ability to pay its short-term debts.
> - A ratio, such as the current ratio or acid test ratio, that measures how easily a business's assets can be turned into cash to cover its short-term liabilities.
> - A measure of a business's ability to meet its short-term financial obligations using its current assets
> - $\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{ratio}=\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$
> 
> - $\mathrm{Acid} \mathrm{test}=\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets} \mathrm{inventory}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$

parts.problem_md: Define the term ‘gross profit margin’.
parts.solution_md:
Gross profit margin is a profitability ratio **[1]** that shows gross profit as a percentage of revenue **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A profitability ratio that compares gross profit (profit before the deduction of overheads/expenses) with revenue, usually expressed as a percentage.
> - A measure showing how much gross profit a business makes for every dollar of revenue, calculated as gross profit divided by revenue.
> - The percentage of revenue remaining after cost of sales has been deducted, but before other expenses are taken away
> - $\mathrm{Gross} \mathrm{profit} \mathrm{margin}=\frac{\mathrm{Gross} \mathrm{Profit}}{\mathrm{Total} \mathrm{Revenue}(\mathrm{Sales})}\times100$

parts.problem_md: Discuss the view that profitability ratios are more important than liquidity ratios to a business that sells expensive jewellery.
parts.solution_md:
Profitability ratios are likely to be very useful to a business selling expensive jewellery **[E]**, as it should have a high gross profit margin due to the large mark-up on luxury items **[Ap]**. This shows how well the business is turning its high-value sales into actual profit **[K]**, which is important for judging whether its business model is working **[An]**

However, liquidity ratios cannot be ignored **[E]**. A jewellery business is likely to hold expensive items in inventory for a long time before they sell, since jewellery is not an everyday purchase **[Ap]**. This can make liquidity ratios like the current ratio look artificially strong **[An]**, even though the business may struggle to access cash quickly if it needed to pay suppliers, since so much of its value is tied up in unsold stock **[Ap] [An]**

Overall, I think profitability ratios are particularly important for this type of business **[E]**, because its naturally slow inventory turnover means liquidity ratios can be misleading if looked at alone **[An]**. However, liquidity is still essential, as a business that cannot pay its short-term debts risks being forced to close, no matter how profitable it looks on paper **[An]**. A business would need to look at both types of ratio together, along with trends over time, rather than relying on just one **[E]**

parts.problem_md: Discuss whether the published accounts of a luxury hotel provide a good measure of the performance of the business.

$\mathrm{Acid} \mathrm{test}=\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets}--\mathrm{Inventory}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$

Acid test
